lessons.title: Until the fact stops changing
explanation: Facts attached to a block can flow along CFG edges until nothing new appears. A dataflow fact is a statement about the program at a program point: 'these names are live', 'this pointer may alias that one', 'this name holds a constant'. Each block has an in-set, a transfer (gen/kill), and an out-set. Edges copy the out of a predecessor into the in of a successor, or the reverse for a backward analysis.

CMU 15-411 treats the fixed point as the whole idea. You recompute a block when an incoming fact changed. When a round adds nothing, the fact has settled. Direction is part of the analysis: reaching definitions and available expressions flow forward, from defs toward uses. Liveness flows backward, from uses toward defs.

The worklist is the practical engine. Start with blocks that have a seed fact. When a block's out changes, put its successors (forward) or predecessors (backward) on the list. Do not rescan the whole CFG every time. The diagram's in / gen / kill / out is one step of that loop.
lessons.example: Available-expression analysis seeds `t1 = a + b` as generated in its block. Forward flow carries 'a+b is available' into successors until a kill (a redefinition of `a` or `b`) or the fact stops changing. A later CSE pass reads that settled fact.
lessons.whyItMatters: Global rewrites are only as honest as the fact that reached a fixed point. A one-shot scan of the CFG is not an analysis.

quiz.stem: A dataflow fact is best described as:
quiz.correctAnswer: Something that flows along CFG edges until a fixed point

distractors.text: A source comment the parser copies into the AST
distractors.rationale: Facts live on the CFG, after three-address exists.

distractors.text: A one-time annotation that never updates at joins
distractors.rationale: Joins mix incoming facts; the analysis iterates.

distractors.text: A machine opcode selected for the current operator
distractors.rationale: This is an analysis on IR, not a later selection.

quiz.correctExplanation: In, transfer, out, repeat until nothing moves. That is the fact.
objectiveIds: Describe a dataflow fact as something that flows until a fixed point

quiz.correctAnswer: A name is live from a use back toward the definition that feeds it

distractors.text: Uses are always written before definitions in a block
distractors.rationale: Defs precede uses in a block; liveness still walks against the edges.

distractors.text: Forward flow cannot represent any fact on a CFG
distractors.rationale: Reaching definitions are a forward analysis; direction depends on the question.

distractors.text: The CFG has no predecessors, only successors
distractors.rationale: Edges have both ends; backward means follow predecessors.

quiz.correctExplanation: Need is discovered at the use and pushed toward the def. That is backward.
objectiveIds: Predict whether a given analysis must run forward or backward

quiz.correctAnswer: Forward, from each definition toward the uses it can reach

distractors.text: Backward, because every analysis on a CFG is backward
distractors.rationale: Only questions about future uses (liveness) need backward flow.

distractors.text: In the lexer, before any block exists
distractors.rationale: The fact rides CFG edges, which exist after three-address.

distractors.text: Once per function, ignoring joins and loops
distractors.rationale: Loops and joins are why you iterate to a fixed point.

quiz.correctExplanation: A def sends a fact downstream. Successors receive it until the fact settles.
objectiveIds: Predict whether a given analysis must run forward or backward

lessons.title: A worklist, not a full sweep
explanation: Worklist algorithms keep only the blocks whose facts still moved. Seed the list with every block, or with the ones that have a gen. Pop a block, recompute its out from in and the transfer. If out changed, enqueue the successors (forward) or the predecessors (backward). When the list is empty, every edge has a consistent fact. That is the fixed point.

Direction is still the first design choice. Available expressions and reaching definitions generate a fact at a def and push it along successor edges; a kill stops it. Liveness generates a fact at a use and pushes it along predecessor edges; a def kills it. Mixing the two — running liveness forward — produces a set that does not mean 'still needed'.

Joins need a meet. Forward may-facts usually union the incoming outs: if either predecessor says `t1 = a + b` may be available, the join records the weaker claim, or you take intersection for a must-fact such as 'definitely available on every path'. The meet is part of the analysis, not an afterthought. Loops just make the worklist revisit a block when the back-edge carries a new value.

Monotone frameworks are why this terminates. If each transfer only adds (or only removes) information in a finite lattice, the fact cannot climb forever. Bitvector analyses — liveness, reaching defs — are the usual exhibit. You do not need the lattice lecture to run the worklist; you need to know that 'changed' is well-defined.

The picture of in / gen / kill / out is one block's step. The algorithm is the queue around it. A pass that walks the CFG once and writes an answer has not done dataflow; it has done a local scan and hoped the joins were simple.
lessons.example: Block B gens `{t1}` and kills nothing. After the first visit, out(B) = `{t1}`. Successors go on the worklist. A loop back-edge later brings a larger in-set; B is enqueued again. When out(B) stops growing, B stays off the list.
lessons.whyItMatters: Compile time in a global pass is 'how many times did the worklist wake this block', not 'how pretty is the lattice slide'.

quiz.stem: A worklist dataflow step, when a block's out-set changes, should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Enqueue the block's successors (forward) or predecessors (backward)

distractors.text: Delete the CFG and rebuild it from source tokens
distractors.rationale: The graph stays; only the fact moved.

distractors.text: Stop immediately, because one change means the analysis failed
distractors.rationale: Change is the signal to propagate, not to abort.

distractors.text: Always rescan every block in the function, ignoring the queue
distractors.rationale: That is a full sweep. The worklist exists to avoid it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Only neighbors of a changed out can have a new in. That is the queue.
objectiveIds: Describe a dataflow fact as something that flows until a fixed point

quiz.stem: Available expressions run forward; liveness runs backward. Mixing them would:
quiz.correctAnswer: Compute a set that no longer means 'available' or 'still needed'

distractors.text: Always produce the same bitvectors, because CFG edges are undirected
distractors.rationale: Edges are directed; direction is the analysis.

distractors.text: Be required, because every fact must travel both ways
distractors.rationale: Each question has one honest direction.

distractors.text: Move the analysis into the parser, where direction does not matter
distractors.rationale: These facts live on the CFG of three-address code.

quiz.correctExplanation: Forward gens at defs. Backward gens at uses. Swap them and the bits lose their meaning.
objectiveIds: Predict whether a given analysis must run forward or backward

quiz.stem: A one-shot walk of the CFG that never requeues a block after a join is not dataflow because:
quiz.correctAnswer: A later incoming fact from a loop or second predecessor can still change the result

distractors.text: Dataflow forbids using the CFG at all
distractors.rationale: The CFG is the highway the fact travels.

distractors.text: One-shot walks are how liveness is defined in the literature
distractors.rationale: Liveness iterates; a single reverse sweep is only a starting heuristic.

distractors.text: Joins are parsed as tokens and never appear as edges
distractors.rationale: Joins are CFG edges after three-address exists.

quiz.correctExplanation: Fixed point means 'no incoming fact can still move the out-set'. One walk cannot promise that.
objectiveIds: Describe a dataflow fact as something that flows until a fixed point

lessons.title: Still needed on the way out
explanation: Live names are the ones a later instruction still needs. A name is live at a point if there is a path from that point to a use that does not redefine it first. The analysis is backward: a use gens the name; a def kills it. Live-out of a block is the union of live-in of successors. Live-in is (live-out minus defs) plus uses.

A short block `t2 = t1 * c; return t2` has `t2` used at the return, so `t2` is live just before the return and dead before its def. `t1` and `c` are live on entry because the multiply uses them. A name that is written and never used is not live anywhere after the write: there is no path to a use.

That last fact is why dead-code elimination reads liveness. If `t9 = a + b` has no live use of `t9`, the add is dead. A later pass deletes it. Here the job is the sets: what is live on entry to this block, and why a never-used name does not appear.
lessons.example: Block: `t1 = a + b; t2 = t1 * c; return t2`. Live-in is `{a, b, c}`. `t1` is live between its def and the multiply, not on entry. `t9` defined in another block and never used is not in any live set.
lessons.whyItMatters: A pass that keeps a value 'just in case' is paying for a name that liveness already proved nobody reads.

quiz.stem: In `t1 = a + b; t2 = t1 * c; return t2`, which names are live on entry?
quiz.correctAnswer: `a`, `b`, and `c`; `t1` and `t2` are defined in the block

distractors.text: `t1` and `t2` only, because those are the temporaries
distractors.rationale: They are defined here; live-in cares about uses of names not yet defined.

distractors.text: No names, because a backward analysis starts empty and stays empty
distractors.rationale: The return uses `t2`, which pulls `t1` and then `a,b,c` backward.

distractors.text: Every name in the function, including unused `t9`
distractors.rationale: Unused names have no path to a use, so they are not live.

quiz.correctExplanation: Walk backward from `return t2`. Kill `t2` at its def, kill `t1` at its def, leave `{a,b,c}`.
objectiveIds: Compute which names are live on entry to a short block

quiz.stem: A value that is never used is not live because:
quiz.correctAnswer: There is no path from its definition to a use that still needs it

distractors.text: The verifier rejects any unused name as ill-formed SSA
distractors.rationale: Unused SSA names can be well-formed; they are just dead.

distractors.text: Forward reaching-defs already deleted it
distractors.rationale: Liveness, not reaching defs, is the 'still needed' fact.

distractors.text: Three-address forbids naming a result you might not read
distractors.rationale: You can name it; liveness then shows nobody reads it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Live means a future use. No use, not live, anywhere after the write.
objectiveIds: Predict why a value that is never used is not live

quiz.stem: `t9 = a + b` with no later use of `t9` contributes to liveness how?
quiz.correctAnswer: It does not make `t9` live; `a` and `b` are live just before the add

distractors.text: `t9` is live throughout the function as a result name
distractors.rationale: Without a use, `t9` is dead after the def.

distractors.text: The add is live-out of every successor, so `t9` stays live
distractors.rationale: Live-out comes from successor uses, and there are none of `t9`.

distractors.text: Liveness cannot see names invented by three-address
distractors.rationale: Temporaries are exactly the names the sets hold.

quiz.correctExplanation: `t9` has no use, so it is not live. The operands are live at the add.
objectiveIds: Predict why a value that is never used is not live

lessons.title: May these two pointers meet
explanation: Pointers that might designate the same location are a may-alias pair. Alias analysis answers that question conservatively: 'must not', 'must', or the usual 'may'. Two allocas in the same function with no pointer arithmetic that could overlap must not alias. A pointer argument and a global may alias unless provenance says otherwise. 'Don't know' is may.

The fact is a dataflow (and interprocedural) product because stores and pointer copies move the relationship around. A `store p, q` can make later loads through `q` see what `p` wrote. If the analysis says they may alias, a pass that wants to reorder a load past a store cannot. That reorder is the transformation that becomes illegal.

Must-alias is rarer and stronger: the two pointers are the same location on every path. Most clients only need the may/must-not cut. LLVM's alias queries are this cut. Over-approximating may-alias is safe and pessimistic; under-approximating it (claiming must-not when they might meet) is a miscompile.
lessons.example: `t1 = load p; store 0, q; t2 = load p`. If `p` and `q` may alias, `t2` might not equal `t1`; CSE of the loads is illegal. If they must not alias, the store cannot touch `*p` and the second load can reuse `t1`.
lessons.whyItMatters: Almost every load-store rewrite is an alias question in disguise. Wrong must-not is a silent miscompile.

quiz.correctAnswer: They might designate the same location on some path the analysis cannot rule out

distractors.text: They have the same SSA name, so they are the same value
distractors.rationale: Equal names are must-alias of a trivial kind; may-alias is about possibly distinct pointers.

distractors.text: They appear in different functions, which always share storage
distractors.rationale: Different functions do not by themselves prove overlap.

distractors.text: The CFG has a join, which merges all pointers into one location
distractors.rationale: Joins merge control, not pointer identity.

quiz.correctExplanation: May means 'the analysis cannot prove they are distinct'. That is the conservative yes.
objectiveIds: Decide whether two pointers may designate the same location

quiz.stem: When `p` and `q` may alias, which rewrite becomes illegal?
quiz.correctAnswer: Reusing `t1 = load p` after `store 0, q` as if `*p` could not have changed

distractors.text: Deleting a never-used add of two constants in another block
distractors.rationale: That add does not touch memory; alias does not apply.

distractors.text: Renaming `x1` to `x2` in SSA inside a single block
distractors.rationale: Pure SSA renaming does not need alias.

distractors.text: Splitting a basic block at a branch, keeping the same loads
distractors.rationale: The CFG split does not reorder a load past a store.

quiz.correctExplanation: The store might write `*p`. The second load is not the same value.
objectiveIds: Name a transformation that becomes illegal if they may alias

quiz.stem: `p` points at a non-escaping alloca and `q` is a different alloca. They:
quiz.correctAnswer: Must not alias, so a store through `q` cannot invalidate `load p`

distractors.text: May alias, because all allocas share one anonymous stack slot
distractors.rationale: Distinct allocas are distinct locations unless a derived pointer mixes them.

distractors.text: Must alias, because both live in the same function
distractors.rationale: Same function is not same location.

distractors.text: Are not pointers, so alias analysis refuses the query
distractors.rationale: Allocas produce addresses; the query is exactly about those.

quiz.correctExplanation: Two private slots, no derived mix. Must-not. The load can stay.
objectiveIds: Decide whether two pointers may designate the same location

lessons.title: Who might call whom
explanation: Who might call whom is a graph the interprocedural passes walk. Nodes are functions. An edge `f → g` means some call in `f` might execute `g`. Direct calls `call g` add a precise edge. The graph is built from the calls that might run, not from the source include graph and not from the CFG inside one function — though each call sits in some block of that CFG.

An indirect call `call t4` where `t4` is a function pointer makes the graph conservative. If the analysis cannot bound `t4`, the node gains edges to every address-taken function of a matching type, or to an unknown node that poisons callees. That over-approximation is why inlining and interprocedural constant prop suddenly go quiet around callbacks.

Recursion is a cycle. A call graph with a cycle is still a call graph; it just means 'do not assume a finite unroll of g from f'. CMU 15-411 treats the call graph as the CFG's cousin across functions. Later inlining reads it. Here the job is to draw the edges you can defend.
lessons.example: `f` contains `call g` and `call t` where `t` is a parameter. The graph has a precise `f → g` and a conservative bundle `f → {every matching address-taken function}` unless a prior analysis narrowed `t`.
lessons.whyItMatters: A missing edge is a miscompile waiting for IPA. An extra edge is only pessimism. Draw the extra one.

quiz.stem: Build the call graph for `f` with a direct `call g` and no other calls:
quiz.correctAnswer: A node `f`, a node `g`, and a single edge `f → g`

distractors.text: A CFG of `f`'s basic blocks, with `g` as a join node
distractors.rationale: That is `f`'s control-flow graph, not the call graph.

distractors.text: An edge from every function in the module to `g`
distractors.rationale: Only callers of `g` get the edge.

distractors.text: No edges, because calls are not three-address instructions
distractors.rationale: Calls are IR instructions; they are exactly the edges.

quiz.correctExplanation: One direct call, one edge. The CFG inside `f` is a different graph.
objectiveIds: Build a call graph from the calls that might execute

quiz.stem: An indirect `call t4` with no bound on `t4` makes the graph conservative because:
quiz.correctAnswer: `f` may need edges to every matching address-taken function, or to unknown

distractors.text: Indirect calls are deleted before the call graph is built
distractors.rationale: They are the hard case; they stay and widen the graph.

distractors.text: The CFG already named the unique callee at the branch
distractors.rationale: A function pointer is not a CFG successor.

distractors.text: The lexer treated `t4` as a keyword, so no edge is required
distractors.rationale: This is IR, not tokens.

quiz.correctExplanation: Unknown target means extra edges. Missing one would hide a real callee.
objectiveIds: Predict how an indirect call makes the graph conservative

quiz.stem: A cycle `f → g → f` in the call graph means:
quiz.correctAnswer: The functions may recurse; the graph is still well-formed

distractors.text: The call graph is illegal and must be flattened into a CFG
distractors.rationale: Cycles are ordinary recursion, not a malformed graph.

distractors.text: Every indirect call has been resolved to a unique callee
distractors.rationale: A cycle says nothing about indirect-call precision.

distractors.text: Three-address form has been lost and must be rebuilt
distractors.rationale: The call graph sits on top of IR; it does not undo it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Recursion is a cycle. Draw it. Do not pretend the callees form a tree.
objectiveIds: Build a call graph from the calls that might execute

lessons.title: Order, dirt, and invalidation
explanation: Pass order is a schedule, and a rewrite can trash the analysis the next pass wanted. A pass manager runs transforms and analyses in sequence, records which analyses are still valid, and reruns a checker when a transform might have broken SSA or types. LLVM and GCC both spend real code on this bookkeeping. The IR verifier after a dirtying pass is not optional taste.

One pass invalidates another pass's analysis when it changes the facts that analysis cached. Inlining adds blocks and calls; the old call graph and the old alias set for the caller are stale. mem2reg deletes loads; a memory-dependence analysis computed before it is a lie. Constant folding rarely dirties dominance; a CFG-restructuring pass always does.

A safe order when a transform dirties SSA or alias facts is: rewrite, verify, then recompute the analyses the next pass will read. Running CSE on alias facts from before a batch of stores were inserted is how you 'prove' two loads are common when a store now sits between them. The manager's job is to refuse that stale read.
lessons.example: mem2reg then CSE is a sane pair: promotion exposes SSA names, then CSE walks use-def. CSE then mem2reg wastes the first CSE on loads that promotion is about to delete. After inlining, alias and the call graph are dirty until recomputed.
lessons.whyItMatters: A 'missed optimization' is often a stale analysis, not a missing idea. The manager is where that staleness is supposed to be named.

quiz.stem: Inlining invalidates a prior alias analysis of the caller because:
quiz.correctAnswer: The callee body injects new loads, stores, and pointers the old facts never saw

distractors.text: Inlining is a parser rewrite and cannot touch IR facts
distractors.rationale: Inlining is an IR transform; it changes the function.

distractors.text: Alias facts are immutable once SSA form exists
distractors.rationale: SSA does not freeze alias; new memory ops still matter.

distractors.text: The verifier deletes alias analysis as illegal IR
distractors.rationale: The verifier checks well-formedness; it does not store alias sets.

quiz.correctExplanation: New memory operations, new pointers. The cached may-alias set is stale.
objectiveIds: Explain why one pass can invalidate another pass's analysis

quiz.stem: A transform that rewrites φs and may break dominance should be followed by:
quiz.correctAnswer: IR verification, then a fresh dominance (and SSA) analysis before the next client

distractors.text: CSE immediately, using the pre-transform dominance tree
distractors.rationale: That tree may no longer describe the CFG.

distractors.text: Deleting the CFG, because φs are now illegal
distractors.rationale: φs are SSA; you check them, you do not throw the graph away.

distractors.text: A lexer rerun on the original source file
distractors.rationale: The dirt is in IR, not in tokens.

quiz.correctExplanation: Dirty SSA wants a verifier, then new analyses. Stale dominance is a miscompile seed.
objectiveIds: Predict a safe order when a transform dirties SSA or alias facts

quiz.stem: CSE that reused a load across a store the previous pass just inserted is a failure of:
quiz.correctAnswer: Invalidation: CSE read alias or memory facts that the store-inserting pass dirtied

distractors.text: Three-address form, which cannot represent loads
distractors.rationale: Loads are ordinary IR; the bug is stale facts.

distractors.text: Verification, which should have rejected well-typed loads
distractors.rationale: The IR can be well-formed and still have a stale analysis.

distractors.text: Liveness, which must run forward after every store
distractors.rationale: The missing update is alias/memory, not liveness direction.

quiz.correctExplanation: The transform dirtied memory facts. CSE needed a rerun, not the old cache.
objectiveIds: Explain why one pass can invalidate another pass's analysis
